title: 2 Chronicles 6:1–11
context: Solomon answers the cloud with a short poetic saying (6:1–2): the LORD said he would dwell in thick darkness, and Solomon has built him a house to dwell in forever. Turning to bless the standing assembly (6:3–11), he praises the LORD for fulfilling his word to David: God chose Jerusalem and chose David, accepted David’s desire to build a house, but appointed his son to build it. The parallel is 1 Kings 8:12–21, and the promise in view is 2 Samuel 7:12–13 and 1 Chronicles 17:11–12. Parallel differences, stated without harmonization: 2 Chronicles 6:5–6 includes God’s choice of Jerusalem and the statement that he chose no man to be prince before David, where 1 Kings 8:16 mentions only the choice of David; and 2 Chronicles 6:11 speaks of the ark set in the house and of the covenant the LORD made with the children of Israel, where 1 Kings 8:21 speaks of a place set for the ark and of the covenant made with the fathers when he brought them out of Egypt. As on 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Kings 8, this site treats the Davidic covenant as shared ground: both traditions see God keeping his own word and Solomon’s kingship and temple as gifts received rather than achievements claimed.

verses.text: Then Solomon said, “The LORD has said that he would dwell in the thick darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon says the LORD said he would dwell in the thick darkness. Arminian readers note the connection with Sinai, where God was present in thick darkness (Exodus 20:21), and they see God’s nearness joined to his mystery, as the cloud that has just filled the house both reveals and conceals him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the thick darkness as a sign that God remains holy and hidden even as he draws near to his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the saying, as at 1 Kings 8:12, as Solomon’s response to the cloud, affirming both God’s real presence and his transcendence over every house made by human hands.

verses.text: But I have built you a house and home, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon says he has built the LORD a house and home, a place to dwell in forever, where 1 Kings 8:13 speaks of a house of habitation. Arminian readers see his words as hope and devotion offered in response to God’s gracious presence, a gift prepared for the God who has drawn near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “forever” alongside 6:18, where Solomon confesses that heaven cannot contain God, and alongside the warnings of 7:19–22. Shared ground: both traditions read the saying as worship rather than as a claim to confine God, held together with the confession and petitions of the prayer that follows.

verses.text: The king turned his face, and blessed all the assembly of Israel; and all the assembly of Israel stood.
verses.arminianNotes: The king turns his face and blesses the whole assembly of Israel while they stand. Arminian readers see the king acting as a servant of the people before God, gathering them into thanksgiving, and they note the reverent posture of the assembly as it receives the king’s words of blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king’s blessing as leading the covenant people in acknowledging what God has done for them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, parallel to 1 Kings 8:14, as a transition from the cloud to the king’s speech, with the whole people included in the moment.

verses.text: He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father, and has with his hands fulfilled it, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon blesses the LORD, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David and has fulfilled it with his hands. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness displayed in history, where his spoken word and his acts agree, and they read the blessing as grateful acknowledgment of a promise kept.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same pairing of mouth and hands as testimony that God’s purposes do not fail but are brought to pass in his time. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise for God’s faithfulness to his promise, the theme that governs the whole blessing in 6:4–11.

verses.text: ‘Since the day that I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel to build a house in, that my name might be there, and I chose no man to be prince over my people Israel;
verses.arminianNotes: God recalls that since the exodus he chose no city to build a house in and no man to be prince over Israel. Arminian readers see God’s choices unfolding in history, made for the good of his people and the honor of his name, and they note that this verse goes beyond 1 Kings 8:16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stressing that the choice of a place and a ruler belongs to God alone and not to human initiative. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for the double choice of Jerusalem and David in 6:6, and both treat it as covenant history rather than a point of dispute.

verses.text: but now I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there; and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.’
verses.arminianNotes: God says he has now chosen Jerusalem for his name and David to be over his people. Arminian readers see these choices as God’s gracious appointment of a place of worship and a ruler for the sake of his people, with real calls to faithfulness laid on David’s line, as 6:16 will make clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the choices of Jerusalem and David as rooted in God’s own will, compare Psalm 78:68–70 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as vocational and covenantal, concerning a city and a royal house; neither imports here the wider debate about individual election to salvation.

verses.text: Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon recalls that it was in David’s heart to build a house for the name of the LORD. Arminian readers honor David’s desire as genuine devotion, a good intention that God welcomed even though he did not grant David the task, and they see God valuing the heart behind the desire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise honor David’s desire, recorded also at 1 Chronicles 28:2, and see it as a response to God’s grace in his life. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the contrast between David’s wish and God’s appointment of his son, a contrast God himself explains in 6:8–9.

verses.text: But the LORD said to David my father, ‘Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells David that he did well to have it in his heart to build a house for God’s name. Arminian readers see God’s kindness in affirming a desire he would not fulfill through David himself, and they take comfort that God receives sincere intentions even when he directs them elsewhere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God honoring David’s desire while keeping the outcome in his own hands, so that the plan of building remains God’s. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of God’s gentle dealing with his servant, affirming the desire while redirecting its fulfillment to the next generation.

verses.text: nevertheless you shall not build the house, but your son who will come out of your body, he shall build the house for my name.’
verses.arminianNotes: David will not build the house, but his son will build it for God’s name. Arminian readers see God assigning different callings to father and son, and they note that 1 Chronicles 28:3 gives the reason that David was a man of war who had shed blood, a reason not stated in this verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s appointment of the builder as part of his promise to David’s house (2 Samuel 7:12–13; 1 Chronicles 17:11–12). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God directing the work according to his purpose and see Solomon’s building as the fulfillment of that word.

verses.text: “The LORD has performed his word that he spoke; for I have risen up in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon declares that the LORD has performed his word: Solomon has risen in David’s place, sits on the throne of Israel, and has built the house. Arminian readers see Solomon receiving his position as a gift and a trust, and they note that the throne he sits on is one given by the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as testimony that God’s promises are sure and that he fulfills them through ordinary succession and human work. Shared ground: both traditions read Solomon’s words as giving credit to God rather than himself, consistent with the site’s treatment of the Davidic covenant as shared ground.

verses.text: There I have set the ark, in which is the LORD’s covenant, which he made with the children of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon has set the ark in the house, the ark in which is the LORD’s covenant made with the children of Israel. Arminian readers see the covenant at the heart of the house, so that the temple is not simply a royal achievement but a place shaped by God’s relationship with his people and its obligations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant in the ark as the foundation of Israel’s life with God, given by grace after the exodus. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking temple and covenant, and both note by reference that 1 Kings 8:21 speaks of the covenant made with the fathers when God brought them out of Egypt.
